title: Because, Thus, Meanwhile
theme: Signal phrases for cause, effect, and sequence
objectives: I can use signal phrases to show cause and effect, time order, and comparison.
I can find signal phrases in an informational text and tell what each one shows.
I can use the endings -ly and -ward to understand time words.
I can write a short explanation that connects ideas with the right signal phrase.
rationale: Signal phrases are the glue of informational writing. This unit teaches ten of them in three groups: cause and effect (as a result, because of, therefore), time and order (meanwhile, eventually, afterward), and adding, comparing, and giving examples (in contrast, in addition, for example, furthermore). Grade 3 students used simple connectors such as because and then. Grade 4 students need to read and write longer chains of ideas. Because function words cannot be pictured, every word is taught through sentences, a flow diagram, and a passage where each phrase does real work.

words.def: Used to show an effect that came from an earlier cause.
words.ex: The path was icy. As a result, the hikers walked slowly and held the rail.
words.ex2: Maya practiced every day for a month, and as a result she won the spelling bee.
words.nonExample: "I like pizza. As a result, the moon is round" does not work, because one fact does not cause the other.

apps.academic: In science writing, as a result links an event to the change it caused.
apps.spoken: It rained all day, and as a result we stayed inside.
apps.writing: Put as a result before the effect and a comma after it.

cloze.s: The river rose over its banks all night; ___, the town closed three roads by morning.

cloze2.s: Lena left her coat at home on the coldest day, and ___ she shivered through recess.

misuse.s: The ice melted. As a result, the moon was bright.
misuse.why: As a result must join a cause to its effect; melting ice did not make the moon bright.

visual.alt: A row of boxes where a cause arrow leads to an effect box.

words.def: Used to say what caused something to happen.
words.ex: Because of the storm, the school bus came an hour late.
words.ex2: The garden grew so well because of all the rain and sunshine.
words.nonExample: Because of needs a noun after it, so "because of it rained" is not correct.

apps.academic: A history text may say a city grew because of a nearby river.
apps.spoken: We stayed home because of the snow.
apps.writing: Follow because of with a noun, such as the rain or her kindness.

cloze.s: Our picnic moved indoors ___ the thunder rolling over the hills.

cloze2.s: The class cheered ___ the good news that the field trip was still on.

misuse.s: The dog barked because of it saw a squirrel in the yard.
misuse.why: Because of must be followed by a noun, not by a whole sentence.

visual.alt: A box labeled cause with an arrow pointing to a box labeled effect.

words.def: For that reason; used to show what follows from a fact.
words.ex: Plants need light to grow; therefore, we put the seedlings by the window.
words.ex2: The bridge was closed, so we therefore took the long way home.
words.nonExample: "Plants need light. Therefore, I like pizza" does not work, because the second idea does not follow from the first.

apps.academic: In an argument, therefore introduces a conclusion that follows from the evidence.
apps.spoken: It is late; therefore, we should go.
apps.writing: Use therefore after a fact to show the conclusion that comes from it.

cloze.s: The map showed a flood on Main Street; ___ we chose a different road.

cloze2.s: Ice is frozen water; ___, it turns into liquid when it gets warm.

misuse.s: It is pouring rain. Therefore, we will have our picnic on the dry, sunny lawn.
misuse.why: Therefore must show a result that makes sense; pouring rain does not lead to a sunny picnic.

visual.alt: Two boxes joined by an arrow: a fact on the left, a conclusion on the right.

words.def: Used to show that two things are very different.
words.ex: Cats usually avoid water. In contrast, many dogs love to swim.
words.ex2: The desert days are hot; in contrast, the nights can be very cold.
words.nonExample: Apples and pears are both sweet fruit, so in contrast is a poor way to join them.

apps.academic: A science report may say that one metal bends and, in contrast, another snaps.
apps.spoken: I like summer, but in contrast my sister likes winter.
apps.writing: Use in contrast to introduce the second of two things that differ.

cloze.s: Frogs begin life in water; ___, most toads spend their lives on dry land.

cloze2.s: The first book was slow and sad; ___, the second was fast and funny.

misuse.s: Both brothers love soccer; in contrast, they both play on the same team every Saturday.
misuse.why: In contrast shows a difference, but this sentence describes two things that are the same.

visual.alt: Two columns facing each other, showing two things that are different.

words.def: Used to give one more fact or idea.
words.ex: The park has swings. In addition, it has a skate ramp and a pond.
words.ex2: Jorge brought drinks to the picnic; in addition, he brought extra napkins.
words.nonExample: Using in addition to give the opposite idea is not correct.

apps.academic: A report on a country might list its mountains and, in addition, its rivers.
apps.spoken: We need paper, and in addition we need glue.
apps.writing: Use in addition to add a fact that goes in the same direction as the last one.

cloze.s: Our library lends books; ___, it lends games and tools to anyone with a card.

cloze2.s: The teacher said to bring a pencil; ___, bring a water bottle for the long walk.

misuse.s: The pool is open today. In addition, it is closed all week.
misuse.why: In addition adds a matching idea; this sentence adds a fact that contradicts the first.

visual.alt: A center idea with extra ideas branching out from it.

words.def: At the same time that something else is happening.
words.ex: Dad cooked the rice. Meanwhile, I set the table.
words.ex2: The knights waited by the gate; meanwhile, the cooks prepared a feast inside the castle.
words.nonExample: Writing meanwhile for something that happened a week later is not correct.

apps.academic: In a history text, meanwhile can show two events that were happening in different places.
apps.spoken: You wash the dishes; meanwhile, I'll dry them.
apps.writing: Use meanwhile to switch to another event that is happening at the same moment.

cloze.s: The kids washed the car; ___, their dad cleaned out the garage next to them.

cloze2.s: Mom drove to the store while I stayed home; ___, the cat slept on the warm couch.

misuse.s: I ate breakfast on Monday. Meanwhile, I ate dinner on Friday.
misuse.why: Meanwhile shows two things happening at the same time; Monday and Friday are different times.

visual.alt: Two parallel rows of events happening side by side at the same time.

words.def: In the end, after a long time or many steps.
words.ex: The tiny seed eventually grew into a tall oak tree.
words.ex2: We circled the block three times before we eventually found the shop.
words.nonExample: Something that happens in one second does not happen eventually.

apps.academic: A science text might say a river eventually carves a deep canyon through rock.
apps.writing: Use eventually for a result that comes after a long time or many tries.

cloze.s: After weeks of daily practice, Ravi ___ learned to ride his bike without any help.

cloze2.s: The ice cube sat in the sun and ___ turned into a puddle on the sidewalk.

misuse.s: The lamp turned on eventually, the very instant I clicked the switch.
misuse.why: Eventually means after a long time, but the lamp lit instantly.

visual.alt: A line from right now to a long time later, with eventually near the far end.

words.def: At a later time; following what was just said.
words.ex: We played soccer, and afterward we shared orange slices.
words.ex2: Afterward, the whole class wrote thank-you notes to the guest speaker.
words.nonExample: Something you did before the game did not happen afterward.

apps.academic: A lab report tells what you did first and what you measured afterward.
apps.spoken: Let's eat, and afterward we can play.
apps.writing: Use afterward to start the next step in a sequence.

cloze.s: The movie ended at eight, and ___ we walked home under the streetlights.

cloze2.s: Finish your math first; ___ you may read for twenty minutes.

misuse.s: We cleaned our room afterward, so it was already tidy before we started.
misuse.why: Afterward means at a later time, but the cleaning happened first.

visual.alt: A first box with an arrow to a second box that comes later.

words.def: Used to show one case that makes an idea clear.
words.ex: Many animals sleep in winter; for example, bears rest in dens.
words.ex2: Use strong verbs. For example, write "sprinted" instead of "ran fast."
words.nonExample: A sentence that gives no case after for example does not help the reader.

apps.academic: A good paragraph states a claim and then gives an example from the text.
apps.spoken: I like fruit; for example, I eat grapes every day.
apps.writing: Use for example after a general idea to show a clear case of it.

cloze.s: Some plants live in the desert, ___ the cactus, which stores water in its thick stem.

cloze2.s: Choose a healthy snack, ___, an apple or some carrot sticks.

misuse.s: Dogs are loyal pets. For example, the moon travels around Earth.
misuse.why: For example must give a case of the idea just stated; the moon is not an example of loyal pets.

visual.alt: No picture; this phrase is taught with sentences.

words.def: Used to add another point that makes the first stronger.
words.ex: The recipe is easy; furthermore, it takes only ten minutes.
words.ex2: Furthermore, walking to school saves money and keeps students healthy.
words.nonExample: Using furthermore to give the opposite idea would confuse your reader.

apps.academic: In an argument, furthermore adds a second reason that supports the claim.
apps.spoken: It's cheap, and furthermore it's close to home.
apps.writing: Use furthermore for a second reason that builds on the first.

cloze.s: Recycling saves energy; ___, it keeps trash out of landfills for years to come.

cloze2.s: The coach is kind; ___, she knows the game better than anyone in town.

misuse.s: Our school is close to home; furthermore, it is very far away.
misuse.why: Furthermore adds a point that agrees with the first; this one contradicts it.

visual.alt: A main reason with a second, stronger reason added next to it.

passage.title: How a Beaver Changes a Stream
paras: A beaver family can change a whole stream. First, the beavers cut down small trees with their strong front teeth. Then they stack the branches across the water and pack them with mud. Eventually, the stack becomes a dam.

The dam slows the stream, and water backs up behind it. As a result, a pond forms where there was once only a narrow channel. Because of the pond, the beavers can build a lodge with an entrance under the water, which keeps them safe from many predators. Meanwhile, the pond is already changing life around it.

Many animals move in. Frogs lay eggs in the shallow water, and ducks use the pond for food and rest. In addition, plants grow along the edge, where the soil stays wet, and insects make homes in those plants. Furthermore, the pond holds water during dry weeks, so nearby animals can still drink.

Not every change is welcome. In contrast, some farmers lose crops when water covers a field. For example, a dam near a road can flood it. Afterward, people may work with wildlife experts to control the water. Therefore, a beaver dam has both helpful and difficult effects.

qs.why: The beavers cut, stack, and pack mud over many steps before the dam exists.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, why does a pond form?
choices: The dam slows the stream so water backs up behind it.
qs.why: The text says the dam slows the stream and water backs up, and as a result a pond forms.

qs.q: Why might an underwater lodge entrance help beavers?
choices: It makes the lodge warmer in summer.
It makes it harder for many predators to reach them.
It gives them a place to store mud.
qs.why: The text says the entrance keeps beavers safe from many predators.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the pond helps other animals?
choices: Beavers cut small trees with their teeth.
A dam near a road can flood it.
Frogs lay eggs in the shallow water and ducks use the pond for food.
qs.why: Frogs and ducks using the pond show the pond provides homes and food.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the main idea of the passage?
choices: Beavers are the only animals that build.
A beaver dam changes a stream in ways that help some living things and cause problems for others.
Ponds are always better than streams.
Farmers should never live near water.
qs.why: The passage shows how the dam creates a pond, helps animals, and sometimes harms farms.

write.prompt: Explain how one event caused another. Use at least three signal phrases from this unit.

parts.m: in a way that is; at a time that is

study.task: Find the word that ends with -ly or -ward in this unit. Write what the ending adds, then use the word and one other signal phrase in a two-sentence explanation.

groups.label: signal phrases for cause and effect
signal phrases for time and order
signal phrases for adding, comparing, and showing

sentences: Write two sentences about something that happened at school. Use as a result to connect them.
Write a sentence about two animals or two places that are very different. Use in contrast.
Write a sentence that uses because of and a weather word.
Write two sentences about your day, using afterward in the second one.

given: The bus took a different route.
combine.model: The road was flooded; therefore, the bus took a different route.
Our school has a library; in addition, it has a computer lab and a garden.

discuss: Which signal phrase would you use to explain why something happened? Why that one?
How do for example and furthermore help a reader in different ways?
Tell a partner about your morning with meanwhile, afterward, and eventually.
produce.explain: Explain how a signal phrase like as a result helps a reader follow a cause and its effect. Use an example from the beaver passage.

argue.prompt: Claim: Writers should always use signal phrases. Take a side and give two reasons.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. For example, ___.

constructed.prompt: Write about a time when weather changed your plans. Use as a result and because of, and make the cause and effect clear.
look: puts a cause before an effect
makes sense as a short account
constructed.model: Because of the storm, our game was canceled. As a result, we played board games inside and everyone had a good time.

constructed.prompt: Compare two foods or two places. Use in contrast and furthermore in your writing.
constructed.model: Pizza is hot and cheesy. In contrast, a salad is cold and crunchy. Furthermore, a salad has more vegetables than pizza does.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten signal phrases in three groups, read an informational text where each one links ideas, notice the endings -ly and -ward, and write short explanations that connect causes, order, and examples.

notes.va.as-a-result.phr: Put the cause on the left and the effect on the right of a two-box chart. Students often use as a result when nothing caused the second event; ask what the cause was.
notes.va.because-of.phr: Teach the pattern: because of + noun phrase. Contrast with because + a whole clause. Do not over-correct speech; focus on writing.
notes.va.therefore.adv: Therefore signals a conclusion. Have students test it by asking whether the second sentence really follows from the first.
notes.va.in-contrast.phr: Use two-column charts. Students may confuse contrast with compare; in contrast points to a difference.
notes.va.in-addition.phr: In addition adds a matching idea. Do not use it for an opposite idea. Students can chain three facts about a topic.
notes.va.meanwhile.adv: Meanwhile is about two events at the same time. Use a two-row timeline and ask students to place events on it.
notes.va.eventually.adv: Eventually suggests a long time or many steps. Use a seed-to-tree example and ask what would be too quick to be eventually.
notes.va.afterward.adv: Afterward is after + -ward. Practice with a three-step recipe or lab routine and have students retell it.
notes.va.for-example.phr: Always follow for example with a real case. Practice giving two different examples of one general statement.
notes.va.furthermore.adv: Furthermore adds a stronger point in an argument. It is a formal word; students can also use also and in addition in speech.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The dam slows the stream. Water backs up. The text says as a result, a pond forms. As a result tells me the pond is an effect of the dam. I can write my own cause and effect: The path was icy. As a result, we walked slowly.'
discuss: Which signal phrases helped you follow the beaver passage?
How can a missing signal phrase make an explanation harder to follow?
misconceptions: Because of and because mean the same thing in every sentence pattern.
In contrast means to compare two similar things.
For example can be followed by any fact.
extend: Write a four-sentence paragraph about a science event using as a result, meanwhile, and therefore.
Find signal phrases in a textbook page and sort them by what they show.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the cause-and-effect group two days later, again at one week, and ask students to underline signal phrases in their own writing in every later unit.

wida.oral: Partner A states a cause and Partner B finishes the sentence with as a result or therefore and an effect. Then switch roles.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (debido a, en cambio, además, con el tiempo, por lo tanto) not reviewed by a native speaker; eventually versus the false friend eventualmente should be confirmed.
Function-word cloze items allow more than one connector; each carries a context clue, but a teacher should confirm they are not ambiguous for grade 4.
Beaver facts (dam from branches and mud, pond formation, underwater lodge entrance, wildlife using the pond) are common-knowledge facts; confirm against a classroom science source.
